title: ASIC eyes claims and AI among crackdown priorities
full_text:
ASIC eyes claims and AI among crackdown priorities
Misconduct that adds to living cost pressures and consumer harm caused by poorly implemented technologies are among the corporate regulator’s enforcement priorities for next year.
Australian Securities and Investments Commission chair Sarah Court today outlined nine areas of heightened risk where the financial services industry should expect greater scrutiny.
“Our first priority is misconduct that compounds cost-of-living pressures, with particular attention to banks, insurers and superannuation trustees,” she said.
“We will examine pricing promises that are not delivered, discounts that are not passed on, improper fees, poor claims handling and failures to provide hardship support or other entitlements.”
Ms Court warns consumer protection must keep pace with the development of new technology.
The regulator will focus on poorly designed or inadequately supervised systems that produce misleading information, make inappropriate decisions or prevent customers from accessing effective support and assistance.
“Artificial intelligence, automated decision-making and chatbots may improve the delivery of financial services but do not alter a firm’s legal obligations,” Ms Court said.
“The ability to obtain human review is particularly important where customers are making a complaint, responding to a scam, pursuing an insurance claim or seeking financial assistance.”
Other priorities include predatory practices targeting consumers and small businesses in financial difficulty, harmful advice and lead generation models, misconduct by auditors and other professional gatekeepers, and failures in financial reporting, licensing and record-keeping.
The regulator will also focus on misconduct in private credit and managed investment schemes – holding to account those responsible for the collapse of the Shield and First Guardian Master Funds – and exploitation and misuse of ASIC’s corporate registers.
The annual priorities sit alongside the commission’s enduring priorities, including misconduct that threatens market integrity or carries a high risk of significant consumer harm, serious governance failures and systemic compliance failures by large financial institutions.
Ms Court says she remains committed to enforcement that is “visible and consequential”.
“We will distinguish an isolated failure that is identified and remedied promptly from misconduct that is extended, repeated or systemic,” she said.
“A firm’s response will matter. Effective remediation and genuine co-operation will be relevant, as will any failure to address known risks brought to the attention of senior leaders.”
